titleStmt.title: Telegram From Secretary of State Shultz’s Delegation to the Department of State

div.head: 451. Telegram From Secretary of State Shultz’s Delegation to the Department of State
div.p: Secto 19025. Subject: The Secretary’s meeting with President Sanguinetti of Uruguay.

2. Summary: The Secretary’s meeting with President Sanguinetti addressed the domestic situation in Uruguay, where political conditions have stabilized but labor unrest is on the rise, and the country’s foreign debt and trade problems. Sanguinetti emphasized the need to increase trade and expressed concern about protectionism, especially on the part of the EC, whose agricultural subsidies are undercutting Uruguayan exports. Sanguinetti expressed gratitude for U.S. support for Uruguay’s debt rescheduling and other efforts to help, including the recent modest cheese quota and congressional authorization for dols 30 million in economic assistance in FY 86 and FY 87. The Secretary said he hoped the Congress would appropriate the funds needed to implement the authorization. Foreign Minister Iglesias renewed his proposal for informal private talks with selected leaders on the debt and trade issues; the Secretary described the complexity of the current situation and said the U.S. was carefully studying how best to proceed.

3. On Central America, Sanguinetti said the new Contadora support group was intended to clarify public understanding of the Contadora process and that his government was pressing the Nicaraguans on the issues of Soviet influence and internal democracy. The Secretary asked for continued Uruguayan cooperation on UN issues. Sanguinetti reiterated his desire to accept President Reagan’s invitation for a state visit to Washington; the Secretary explained that the President’s operation and recovery had required
changes in his schedule and the visit had to be rescheduled. Tone of meeting was cordial throughout. End summary.

4. Participants: The Secretary met with President Sanguinetti of Uruguay at 9:00 a.m., Tuesday, September 24, at the Uruguayan UN Mission. The Secretary was accompanied by USUN Ambassador Walters, ARA Assistant Secretary Abrams, ARA/SC Director Durkee note taker, Deputy Press Spokesman Redmond, White House fellow Karen Galatz, and Stephanie van Riegersberg interpreter. President Sanguinetti was accompanied by Foreign Minister Iglesias, UN Ambassador Lupinacci, and Ambassador to the US Luisi.
5. Situation in Uruguay: After opening pleasantries, Sanguinetti offered six-month assessment of developments since last discussion in Montevideo at March inauguration:

list.item: Country was stabilizing, with democratic institutions functioning and political parties cooperating;
Main domestic problem was labor unrest, but this was understandable after twelve years of repression;
Internal dynamic was somewhat unbalanced, with business sector too discouraged and labor leaders too aggressive;

GOU working to restore balance, first by getting agreement on external debt, which has been accomplished through negotiations with IMF, World Bank, and private banks, with next priority to ease domestic debt problems.

div.p: 6. U.S. support for refinancing: The Secretary noted that the US had tried to be supportive of Uruguay’s debt rescheduling; Sanguinetti expressed appreciation for the U.S. efforts.

7. Trade problems: Sanguinetti went on to stress GOU concerns over foreign trade problems, which he described as more important than debt problems. Uruguay’s export earnings were down 10 percent so far in 1985; worse yet, prices of Uruguay’s major export products still declining, thanks to European subsidized competition. He had spoken same morning to French Foreign Minister to explain problem and to insist that EC had to make changes, but no solution in sight. As example, he mentioned that Brazil was offered EC meat at dols 600 per ton, a price that was about half the market price, and Uruguay simply could not compete under such conditions; the EC had 900,000 tons of meat in storage, and that overhang depressed the market.

8. U.S. support on trade: The Secretary agreed that European agricultural policies caused serious distortions and encouraged Sanguinetti to continue to make that point to EC leaders. He noted that the U.S. had opened up the U.S. cheese market to Uruguay through a modest quota, and added his hope that the Congress would provide the appropriation needed to implement the authorization for ESF for Uruguay. Sanguinetti expressed understanding of the difference between authorizations and appropriations.

9. Congressional visits: The Secretary said we had encouraged congressional leaders to visit Uruguay and were pleased that Senator Lugar had returned with very positive impressions. Sanguinetti agreed that such visits were very useful to gain clear understanding of complexity of managing transition following long period of dictatorship. Radical rhetoric was to be expected in such conditions, but Uruguayan voters had demonstrated moderation. This tendency was reinforced by positive Argentine example.

10. New GATT round: The Secretary expressed
appreciation for GOU support for new GATT round, noting that best defense against protectionist pressures was good offense in favor of opening markets to trade. The U.S. still offers world’s most open market, and we want other countries to open theirs as well, in order to provide quote level playing field unquote. Sanguinetti said GOU had similar view of objectives but was concerned about pace of events. The situation in Latin America could change quickly, as in Mexican and Peruvian cases, and it was important not to lose more time.

11. Informal debt dialogue: Iglesias recalled discussion in Montevideo regarding possible informal, private discussions about approaches to trade and debt problems, noting that the U.S. had concentrated on strengthening the international financial institutions. This was important but more needed to be done, since new money infusions from private banks were declining sharply. Quiet, informal discussions could help clarify thinking on new approaches and improve coordination. The Secretary said he understood the point and USG was working hard to find practical solutions. Respective roles of IMF and IBRD had to be clarified. Public perception of lead role of IMF led to misconception that debt problem could be resolved through monetary adjustments, when in fact debt problems needed to be addressed in ways in which World Bank was key factor. Debt-ridden countries did not need more debt but rather more equity, which meant that more had to be done to attract capital, especially capital from the affected countries that had gone abroad. These were complex questions, and the U.S. continued to study how best to address them.

12. Central America: Recalling Ambassador Shlaudeman’s recent visit to Montevideo and other capitals of the Contadora support group, the Secretary asked for Uruguayan views of Central American situation. Sanguinetti replied that GOU supported the Contadora process and wanted new support group to be helpful. New initiatives were sometimes misunderstood, as when the Cartagena group was initially misperceived as a debtors cartel, but Contadora support group was intended to
clarify public understanding in Latin America of Central American issues. For GOU, avoiding armed conflict in Central America was domestic issue as well as foreign policy problem. The GOU has pressed Nicaragua, most recently in discussions with VP Ramirez, on two key points: First, Soviet influence is very negative; second, there must be progress toward internal democracy. Ramirez understands these points, but the commandantes have the power. The GOU understands the U.S. position that there will be no military intervention but U.S. will support those forces putting pressure on Sandinistas. It was very important that such activities be perceived as consistent with international principles and standards of conduct, since small countries were often forced to depend on such principles more than major powers.
The Secretary expressed appreciation for the Uruguayan comments and said we wanted to stay in close touch through Ambassador Shlaudeman.

13. UN affairs: The Secretary explained that the U.S. took seriously what happened at the UN, for which reason we had assigned one of our best Ambassadors. We appreciate past cooperation with the GOU and looked forward to working closely with them at this session of the UNGA.

14. State visit: Sanguinetti said he had very much appreciated President Reagan’s kind words on receiving the credentials of Ambassador Luisi. He reiterated his desire to accept the invitation to visit Washington. The Secretary said we were looking forward to that visit and explained that the President’s unexpected surgery and need to recuperate had disrupted his schedule. The President has recovered well, but the visit has had to be
rescheduled for later.

note.p: Source: Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D850684–0008. Confidential; Immediate; Exdis. Sent for information Immediate to Montevideo.

In telegram 2980 from Brasilia, March 22, the Embassy reported on Bush’s March 15 meeting with Sanguinetti in Brasilia, in which Bush responded to a “request for U.S. help with Uruguay’s international creditors” by expressing “understanding of Sanguinetti’s position and our desire to help our friends, but pointed to the limits placed on the United States ability to be helpful by the current deficit.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D850198–0111)

In telegram 3915 from Montevideo, July 8, the Embassy described Senator Richard Lugar’s (R–IN) July 2 visit and meeting with Sanguinetti. (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D850480–0276)

In telegram 10444 from Lima, September 13, the Embassy reported on Shlaudeman’s September 11 meeting with Iglesias about Central America. (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D850652–0597)
Reagan hosted an Oval Office ceremony to receive diplomatic credentials from Ambassadors including Luisi. Reagan’s remarks have not been found. (Public Papers: Reagan, 1985, Book II, p. 1516)
